text: Dawn, August twenty-fourth, eighteen seventy-seven. In the Lower Geyser Basin, a group of tourists from Montana is camped near Fountain Geyser. They've been in the park ten days, enjoying the sights.

That morning, riders appear out of the steam. They are [Nez Perce](/nˌɛz pˈɜɹs/) warriors. And behind them, crossing the world's first national park, are about eight hundred men, women and children, with nearly two thousand horses, running from the United States Army.

Before the day is over, one of those tourists, George Cowan, will be shot in the leg and then in the head, and left for dead in the forest. He will survive. He will crawl about twelve miles over four days.

This is the story of the thirteen days when a war crossed Yellowstone. The Park Service says it may be the only war ever fought inside an existing national park. And of the people the Army was chasing, who were not invaders here, but families trying to save their own lives.
The [Nez Perce](/nˌɛz pˈɜɹs/) call themselves the [nimíipuu](/nimˈiːpuː/), "the people." Their homeland stretched across what is now Oregon, Idaho and Washington.

In eighteen sixty-three, the United States rewrote an earlier treaty and cut their reservation by about ninety percent. Many [Nez Perce](/nˌɛz pˈɜɹs/) never agreed to it. They still call it the Thief Treaty.

One band was led by a chief the Americans called Joseph. His own name was [Hinmatóowyalahtq̓it](/hɪnmətˈuːjəlɑːtkɪt/). His band refused to give up its home in Oregon's [Wallowa](/wɑlˈaʊə/) Valley, as his father had refused before him. In the spring of eighteen seventy-seven, the Army ordered them onto the smaller reservation. Before they could get there, violence broke out, and war followed.
So five bands of [Nez Perce](/nˌɛz pˈɜɹs/) did the only thing they could. They ran. Over the mountains into Montana, hoping to find safety with the Crow, and later hoping to reach Canada.

On August ninth, at a place called the Big Hole, soldiers attacked their camp at dawn. Many [Nez Perce](/nˌɛz pˈɜɹs/) were killed, including women and children. The survivors kept moving south and east. Straight toward Yellowstone.

This is Henrys Lake, in Idaho, just west of the park. On August twentieth, near here, [Nez Perce](/nˌɛz pˈɜɹs/) warriors raided the Army's camp at night and ran off its pack mules. The general in charge, Oliver Otis Howard, stopped here for days to rest and resupply his men.
Three days later, on August twenty-third, the [Nez Perce](/nˌɛz pˈɜɹs/) entered Yellowstone, near where the West Entrance is today.

Leading them through the park was a man named Poker Joe, also called Lean Elk. He was of mixed descent, spoke English, and knew the country. Leadership was shared among several chiefs, including Looking Glass, a respected war leader. Joseph's role was mostly to care for the camp: the elders, the women and the children.
They followed the Firehole River upstream, through the geyser basins. And that's where they ran into the tourists.

The tourists were nine people from [Radersburg](/ɹˈeɪdɚzbɝɡ/), Montana. Among them were George Cowan, his young wife Emma, and Emma's brother and sister, Frank and Ida Carpenter. They had come to see the geysers.
The warriors took their horses and supplies and forced them to come along. The party's wagon was abandoned in the forest along what's now called [Nez Perce](/nˌɛz pˈɜɹs/) Creek.

At first, Poker Joe tried to protect them. The tourists thought he was Chief Joseph himself. He offered to let them go in exchange for their horses and guns, and he warned them that some of the younger warriors were angry.
At the base of Mary Mountain, those warnings came true. George Cowan was shot through the thigh, then in the head. He was left for dead.

He wasn't dead. When he woke up, he started to crawl. For four days, wounded, he dragged himself about twelve miles through the forest, until scouts riding ahead of General Howard's army finally found him on August twenty-ninth.

Meanwhile, the [Nez Perce](/nˌɛz pˈɜɹs/) held a council about the captives. On August twenty-fifth, near Mud Volcano, they let Emma, Ida and Frank go free. Poker Joe himself rode with them to the river, and pointed them toward safety.
Years later, Emma Cowan wrote about that summer. She remembered the terror. But she also remembered moments of kindness from the people who held her.
That same evening, the whole [Nez Perce](/nˌɛz pˈɜɹs/) caravan crossed the Yellowstone River at a shallow place near Mud Volcano. Today, it's called [Nez Perce](/nˌɛz pˈɜɹs/) Ford.
Picture it. Hundreds of people, elders and children, nearly two thousand horses, all crossing the river at dusk, with the Army somewhere behind them.

Not every encounter went the way of the Cowans'. On August twenty-sixth, near Otter Creek, close to the Grand Canyon of the Yellowstone, warriors attacked another group of tourists from Helena. A man named Charles Kenck was killed. Another, Jack Stewart, was wounded and robbed. A third, Ben Stone, survived by hiding in the creek until nightfall.

Five days later, at Mammoth, a warrior killed another member of that group, Richard Dietrich, in the doorway of a cabin. The man who fired had lost his own family at the Big Hole, just three weeks earlier.
That same day, warriors raided a ranch a few miles below Mammoth and burned the house. Cavalry and Crow scouts arrived soon after.
In all, the [Nez Perce](/nˌɛz pˈɜɹs/) met about twenty-five visitors in Yellowstone. Two were killed.
General Howard followed them into the park with about six hundred men, but he never caught up. He never fought them anywhere inside Yellowstone.

The [Nez Perce](/nˌɛz pˈɜɹs/) moved east through Pelican Valley and into the high country of the northeast. Another Army column, under Colonel Samuel Sturgis, waited to trap them at the edge of the mountains.

Instead, the [Nez Perce](/nˌɛz pˈɜɹs/) made a feint, drawing Sturgis away. Then they slipped out through a narrow gorge to the Clarks Fork River, through a gorge said to be barely wide enough for two horses side by side. By the time Sturgis realized what had happened and rejoined Howard, the soldiers were two days and about fifty miles behind. The [Nez Perce](/nˌɛz pˈɜɹs/) had spent thirteen days in Yellowstone. And they were still free.
They kept going north for another month. By the end, they had traveled about eleven hundred and seventy miles.
At the end of September, in the Bears Paw Mountains of Montana, they stopped to rest. They were about forty miles from Canada. Another Army force, under Colonel Nelson Miles, attacked.

The siege lasted five days, in freezing cold. Poker Joe was killed. So was Joseph's brother, [Ollokot](/ˈɑləkɑt/). So was Looking Glass, shot when he stepped up onto a bluff to look out over the field.

On October fifth, eighteen seventy-seven, Joseph handed over his rifle. More than four hundred [Nez Perce](/nˌɛz pˈɜɹs/) surrendered. That night, another chief, White Bird, slipped away with a small group, and a few hundred [Nez Perce](/nˌɛz pˈɜɹs/) in all eventually reached Canada.
You may know the words Joseph is said to have spoken that day: "From where the sun now stands, I will fight no more forever."

The truth is more complicated. Those words were written down, and rewritten many times, by an Army officer named Charles Erskine Scott Wood. One historian counted nineteen published versions. But people who were there agreed that Joseph said something very close to that last line.

The survivors were not allowed to go home. Four hundred and thirty-two of them were sent first to Fort Leavenworth, in Kansas, then to Indian Territory, in what is now Oklahoma, where many of the newborns and elders died. Only in eighteen eighty-five were they allowed back to the Northwest, and Joseph was never allowed to return to his [Wallowa](/wɑlˈaʊə/) Valley. He died in nineteen-oh-four on the Colville Reservation in Washington. The Park Service describes him as dying brokenhearted, an exile from his home.

Today, the route of the [Nez Perce](/nˌɛz pˈɜɹs/) is a National Historic Trail, and the [Nez Perce](/nˌɛz pˈɜɹs/) National Historical Park preserves places across four states. Many [Nez Perce](/nˌɛz pˈɜɹs/) consider the trail sacred, and they still come to Yellowstone to honor their ancestors.
A [Nez Perce](/nˌɛz pˈɜɹs/) leader, Rebecca Miles, put it simply, looking back on that history: "There's no future without forgiveness."
So the next time you drive past the Firehole River, or cross the Yellowstone near Mud Volcano, remember: this wasn't empty wilderness. People were here, and some of them were running for their lives.
Thanks for watching Yellowstone, in three parts. The complete story, all three chapters together, is coming to our podcast. See you in the next park.
